To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the thrombus in the left ventricular apex of patients who survive an acute anterior myocardium infarction and are discharged from the hospital resolves more rapidly with oral anticoagulation than with aspirin, and that the thrombus resolves more rapidly with aspirin than with no antithrombolytic therapy.

long-term antithormobotic therapy with either oral anticoagulation or aspirin can reduce the size of left ventricular thrombosis and prevent systemic emboli in patients with anterior myocardial infraction.
the thrombus resolved completely in 12 (60%) patients in the aspirin group, 9 (45%) patients in the anticoagulant group, and 2 (10%) in the control group.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the effects of long-term oral antithrombotics on left ventricular apical thrombus in patients after acute myocardial infraction.
the study of the effects of antithrombotics on left ventricular mural thrombi after acute anterior wall myocardial infarctions.
the effects of long-term antiplatelet therapy on the left ventricular thrombosis.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the long-term antithombotic treatment is beneficial in the prevention of systemic embolism in patients with left ventricular aneurysm and thrombus.
the long-term antithro-mbotic treatment is effective and beneficial to patients with LV aneurysm, especially in patients with large LV thrombus.
the long-term effects of antithrombotics on left ventricular mural thrombi are as follows: anticoagulents are effective, aspirin is less effective, and no antithrombics is least effective.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
long-term antithomobotic treatment with warfarin or aspirin can reduce the size and/or resolve left ventricular thrombosis in patients with anterior wall myocardial infarctions.
the long-term antithro-mbotic therapy with aspirin or oral anticoagulant is effective in reducing the size of left ventricular thrombosis after myocardial infarct.

we have shown that anticoagulation therapy is superior to aspirin therapy and that aspirin is superior to no therapy for the prevention of recurrent thromboembolism in patients with left ventricular thrombosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of antithrombotics on LV thrombi are similar in patients who are treated with aspirin and warfarin, but that both drugs are better than placebo.
we can now measure the effects of antithrombotics on the left ventricular thrombosis.
the use of anticoagulation in patients with left ventricular thrombosis after myocardial infarcts is not as important as previously thought.
